{{Short description|Probabilistic logic}}
A '''Markov logic network''' ('''MLN''') is a [[probabilistic logic]] which applies the ideas of a [[Markov network]] to [[first-order logic]], defining probability distributions on [[possible world]]s on any given [[Domain of discourse|domain]].

==History==
In 2002, [[Ben Taskar]], [[Pieter Abbeel]] and [[Daphne Koller]] introduced relational Markov networks as templates to specify [[Markov networks]] abstractly and without reference to a specific [[Domain of discourse|domain]].<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Cozman |first=Fabio Gagliardi |chapter=Languages for Probabilistic Modeling Over Structured and Relational Domains |date=2020 |title=A Guided Tour of Artificial Intelligence Research |pages=247–283|place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-06167-8_9 |isbn=978-3-030-06166-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Taskar |first1=Ben |last2=Abbeel |first2=Pieter |last3=Koller |first3=Daphne |date=2002-08-01 |title=Discriminative probabilistic models for relational data |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/2073876.2073934 |journal=Proceedings of the Eighteenth Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence |series=UAI'02 |location=San Francisco, CA, USA |publisher=Morgan Kaufmann Publishers Inc. |pages=485–492 |isbn=978-1-55860-897-9}}</ref> Work on Markov logic networks began in 2003 by [[Pedro Domingos]] and Matt Richardson.<ref name="Dom2015">{{cite book |title = The Master Algorithm: How machine learning is reshaping how we live. |pages = 246–7 |date = 2015 |first = Pedro |last = Domingos }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite journal |first1 = Matthew |last1 = Richardson |first2 = Pedro |last2 = Domingos |title = Markov Logic Networks |journal = Machine Learning |volume = 62 |issue = 1–2 |pages = 107–136 |year = 2006 |doi = 10.1007/s10994-006-5833-1 |url = http://www.cs.washington.edu/homes/pedrod/papers/mlj05.pdf |doi-access = free }}</ref> Markov logic networks is a popular formalism for [[statistical relational learning]].<ref>{{Cite thesis |title=Building Practical Statistical Relational Learning Systems |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5c51026n |publisher=UC Santa Cruz |date=2023 |language=en |first=Eriq |last=Augustine}}</ref>

==Syntax==
A Markov logic network consists of a collection of [[formula (mathematical logic)|formula]]s from [[first-order logic]], to each of which is assigned a [[real number]], the weight. The underlying idea is that an interpretation is more likely if it satisfies formulas with positive weights and less likely if it satisfies formulas with negative weights.<ref name=":2" />

For instance, the following Markov logic network codifies how smokers are more likely to be friends with other smokers, and how stress encourages smoking:<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marra |first1=Giuseppe |last2=Dumančić |first2=Sebastijan |last3=Manhaeve |first3=Robin |last4=De Raedt |first4=Luc |date=2024-03-01 |title=From statistical relational to neurosymbolic artificial intelligence: A survey |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370223002084 |journal=Artificial Intelligence |volume=328 |article-number=104062 |doi=10.1016/j.artint.2023.104062 |issn=0004-3702|arxiv=2108.11451 }}{{Creative Commons text attribution notice|cc=by4|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370223002084|author(s)=Giuseppe Marra, Sebastijan Dumančić, Robin Manhaeve and Luc De Raedt}}</ref><math display="block">\begin{array}{lcl} 2.0 & :: & \mathrm{smokes}(X) \leftarrow \mathrm{smokes}(Y) \land \mathrm{influences}(X,Y) 
\\ 0.5 & :: & \mathrm{smokes}(X) \leftarrow \mathrm{stress}(X)
\end{array} </math>

== Semantics ==
[[File:Grounded Markov logic network.jpg|thumb|upright=1.7|Markov network induced by the theory from [[Markov logic network#Syntax|Syntax]] to a two-element domain.]]

Together with a given domain, a Markov logic network defines a [[probability distribution]] on the set of all [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretations]] of its predicates on the given domain. The underlying idea is that an interpretation is more likely if it satisfies formulas with positive weights and less likely if it satisfies formulas with negative weights.

For any [[Arity|<math>n</math>-ary]] [[predicate symbol]] <math>R</math> that occurs in the Markov logic network and every [[Arity|<math>n</math>-]][[tuple]] <math>a_1, \dots, a_n</math> of domain elements, <math>R(a_1, \dots, a_n)</math> is a ''grounding'' of <math>R</math>. An ''interpretation'' is given by allocating a  [[Boolean domain|Boolean]] [[truth value]] (''true'' or ''false'') to each grounding of an element. A ''true grounding'' of a formula <math>\varphi</math> in an interpretation with free variables <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math> is a  [[variable assignment]] of <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math> that makes <math>\varphi</math> true in that interpretation.

Then the probability of any given interpretation is [[directly proportional]] to <math>\exp (\sum_{j} w_j n_j)</math>, where <math>w_j</math> is the weight of the <math>j</math>-th sentence of the Markov logic network and <math>n_j</math> is the number of its true groundings.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

This can also be seen as inducing a [[Markov network]] whose nodes are the groundings of the predicates occurring in the Markov logic network. The feature functions of this network are the groundings of the sentences occurring in the Markov logic network, with value <math>e^w</math> if the grounding is true and 1 otherwise (where again <math>w</math> is the weight of the formula).<ref name=":0" />

==Inference==
The probability distributions induced by Markov logic networks can be queried for the probability of a particular event, given by an atomic formula (''marginal inference''), possibly conditioned by another atomic formula.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Sun |first1=Zhengya |last2=Zhao |first2=Yangyang |last3=Wei |first3=Zhuoyu |last4=Zhang |first4=Wensheng |last5=Wang |first5=Jue |date=2017 |title=Scalable learning and inference in Markov logic networks |journal=International Journal of Approximate Reasoning |volume=82 |pages=39–55 |doi=10.1016/j.ijar.2016.12.003 |issn=0888-613X}}</ref>

Marginal inference can be performed using standard Markov network inference techniques over the minimal subset of the relevant Markov network required for answering the query.  Exact inference is known to be [[♯P|#P]]-complete in the size of the domain.<ref name=":2" />

In practice, the exact probability is often approximated.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Venugopal |first=Deepak |date=2017 |title=Advances in Inference Methods for Markov Logic Networks |url=https://www.comp.hkbu.edu.hk/~cib/2017/Dec/iib_vol18no2.pdf#page=15 |journal=IEEE Intelligent Informatics Bulletin |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=13–19}}</ref>  Techniques for approximate inference include [[Gibbs sampling]], [[belief propagation]], or approximation via [[pseudolikelihood]].

The class of Markov logic networks which use only two variables in any formula allows for polynomial time exact inference by reduction to [[weighted model counting]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kuzelka |first=Ondrej |date=2021-03-29 |title=Weighted First-Order Model Counting in the Two-Variable Fragment With Counting Quantifiers |journal=Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research |volume=70 |pages=1281–1307 |doi=10.1613/jair.1.12320  |doi-access=free|issn=1076-9757|arxiv=2007.05619 }}</ref><ref name=":2" />
